summary: Specifies a mapping between X.400 (1988) / ISO 10021 mail and the Internet mail format of RFC 822, for use on the DARPA Internet and in the UK Academic Community. It was replaced by RFC 2156.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1327 describes how a gateway translates mail between the X.400 standard, used by many large organisations, and the RFC 822 format used on the Internet. It says which headers become which X.400 fields, how an X.400 address is written as text, and what is lost or approximated in the process.

questions: convert x.400 mail to internet mail
what is an x.400 to rfc 822 gateway
how are x.400 addresses mapped to internet email
subtitle: How a gateway turns an X.400 message into an Internet mail message, and back again.

tldr.problem: Two large communities used incompatible mail systems, the X.400 message handling standard and the RFC 822 format used on the Internet, and users of one could not exchange mail with users of the other.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a gateway that maps an RFC 822 message and its transport information into an X.400 interpersonal message, and maps X.400 reports, notifications and messages back into RFC 822, with a textual encoding of X.400 originator and recipient addresses.
tldr.outcome: The RFC obsoletes RFCs 987, 1026, 1138 and 1148, and the RFC Editor index lists it as obsoleted by RFC 2156. It is kept here as a record of the original X.400 to RFC 822 mapping.

today: RFC 1327 is a May 1992 standards-track memo, and the RFC Editor index lists it as obsoleted by RFC 2156. It is kept here as a record of the X.400 to RFC 822 mapping that it specified.

sections.title: What the Mapping Is For
sections.content:
The document describes a set of mappings that enable interworking between systems operating the CCITT X.400 1988 Recommendations on Message Handling Systems, also known as ISO/IEC 10021 on the Message Oriented Text Interchange System, and systems using the RFC 822 mail protocol or protocols derived from it. The approach aims to maximise the services offered across the boundary without requiring unduly complex mappings, and the mappings should not require any changes to end systems. It is a revision of RFCs 987, 1026, 1138 and 1148, which it obsoletes, and it should be used when this mapping is performed on the DARPA Internet or in the UK Academic Community.

X.400 defines an Interpersonal Messaging System that makes use of a store and forward Message Transfer System, and the document relates to that interpersonal service rather than to wider uses of X.400. RFC 822 evolved as a messaging standard on the DARPA Internet and specifies an end to end message format, used in conjunction with a number of different message transfer protocol environments: SMTP on the DARPA Internet and other TCP/IP networks, UUCP networks over dial-up telephone lines, parts of Bitnet with EBCDIC encoding, and the JNT Mail Protocol on X.25 networks. The mappings here are appropriate for all of these.

There is a large community using RFC 822 based protocols who will wish to communicate with users of the X.400 service, and conversion will also be needed where a community intends to move to X.400, so a smooth transition is possible. More than one gateway is expected, and this specification enables them to behave consistently, which gives consistent service to users and the best service where a message crosses several gateways.

Five principles underlie the details. The specification should be pragmatic, with no complex mappings required for academic reasons, and subject to that, functionality across a gateway should be as high as possible. It is always a bad idea to lose information in a transformation, and this includes requested services that cannot be fully mapped. All mail gateways operate at exactly one level above the layer on which they conceptually operate, so a gateway that is to transform the objects it works on has to understand the higher level semantics too. Subject to pragmatism, the specification should be reversible, so that a double transformation brings you back to where you started.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is about the software that sits between two mail worlds and moves messages from one to the other. Its guiding rules are simple: keep as much of the service as possible, never throw information away, and make the translation work in both directions.

sections.title: The Two Service Models and the Gateway
sections.content:
The X.400 IPMS abstract service comprises three basic services: origination, reception and management. Management is a local interaction between the user and the service and is not relevant to gatewaying. The other two consist of operations to originate and receive two objects. The first is the IPM, the interpersonal message, which has two components, a heading and a body. The body is structured as a sequence of body parts, which may be basic components such as IA5 text or G3 fax, or further IP messages, and the heading consists of fields holding end to end user information such as subject, primary recipients and importance. The second object is the IPN, the interpersonal notification, which reports the receipt of an IPM at the user agent level.

These services use the Message Transfer abstract service, which provides submission, used by IPMS origination, delivery, used by IPMS reception, and administration, used by IPMS management. Submission and delivery relate to the MTS message, comprising an envelope and content, which carries an IPM or IPN. The envelope has an ID, an originator and a list of recipients, and the message transfer service is refined into the message transfer agent service, which defines the interaction between agents and the procedures for distributed operation.

RFC 822 is based on the assumption of an underlying service, called the 822-MTS service, which provides three basic functions: identification of a list of recipients, identification of an error return address, and transfer of an RFC 822 message. An RFC 822 message consists of a header and content that is uninterpreted ASCII text, and the header is divided into fields, which are the protocol elements.

The author is careful about the gateway model. It would be elegant to map the 822-MTS service onto the MTS service elements and the RFC 822 message onto an IPM, but reality does not fit, and treating the document as the definition of an X.400 access unit does not fit either. The IPM format, the IPMS service elements, the MTS service elements and the MTA service elements on one side are mapped into RFC 822 and the 822-MTS service on the other in a slightly tangled manner, and access to the MTA service elements is minimised. Going from RFC 822 to X.400, a message and its 822-MTS information are always mapped into an IPM. Going from X.400 to RFC 822, a message may be derived from a report, from an IPN or from an IPM.
sections.plainLanguage: X.400 mail is a structured object with a heading and a body, and it travels through a store and forward system with its own envelope. Internet mail is a header and a block of text, moved by whatever transport is underneath. The gateway has to move information between these two shapes.

sections.title: Mapping Addresses Between the Two Worlds
sections.content:
Chapter 4 of the RFC deals with the mapping between X.400 originator and recipient addresses and RFC 822 addresses, which it calls a fundamental gateway component. An X.400 address is structured as a set of attribute value pairs, and it is clearly necessary to be able to encode it in ASCII for gatewaying purposes, with all components encoded, in order to guarantee the return of error messages and to optimise third party replies.

An originator and recipient address has a number of structured and unstructured attributes. For each unstructured attribute a key and an encoding are specified, and structured attributes are mapped onto one or more attribute value pairs. The 1984 and 1988 attributes are listed with a key for each: MTS.CountryName has the key C, MTS.AdministrationDomainName has ADMD, MTS.PrivateDomainName has PRMD, MTS.NetworkAddress has X121, MTS.TerminalIdentifier has T-ID, MTS.OrganizationName has O, MTS.OrganizationalUnitNames.value has OU, MTS.NumericUserIdentifier has UA-ID, and MTS.PersonalName has PN, with the surname, given name, initials and generation qualifier carrying S, G, I and GQ. The 1988 additions include a common name with the key CN, a physical delivery country name with PD-C, a postal code with PD-CODE, a post office box address with PD-BOX and a unique postal name with PD-UNIQUE. Each attribute also carries a reference to the relevant section of the X.402 standard and, for attributes that exist only in 1988, an extension identifier.

Chapter 4 also covers the EBNF that maps an RFC 822 address onto an X.400 address and back, the mapping of directory names, the mappings for the message transfer service, and the mappings for the interpersonal service. Repeated mappings are also considered, which is often essential, particularly for distribution lists, though in general this leads to a level of service that is the lowest common denominator, roughly the services offered by RFC 822.
sections.plainLanguage: An X.400 address is a set of labelled parts, such as country, organisation and personal name, and each part gets a short key so that it can be written in plain text. The RFC lists the keys and the rules for turning an Internet address into that set and back again.

sections.title: Mapping the Message Itself
sections.content:
Going from RFC 822 to X.400, a single IP message is generated from the RFC 822 message, the RFC 822 headers are used to generate the IPMS heading, and the IP message has one IA5 body part containing the RFC 822 message body. Some RFC 822 fields cannot be mapped onto a standard IPM heading field, so an extension field is defined to carry them, and the message is submitted to the message transfer service with the required services specified in the submission envelope. A few parameters of the message transfer agent abstract service are also specified, so that RFC 822 level parameters can be carried in the analogous X.400 service elements.

The heading fields are generated from the standard RFC 822 headers. Date and Received are ignored, because they are handled at the message transfer service and agent levels. Message-Id is mapped to the identifier of the IPM. From is mapped to the authorizing users if a Sender header is present, and otherwise to the originator. Sender is mapped to the originator, Reply-To to the reply recipients, To to the primary recipients, Cc to the copy recipients, and Bcc to the blind copy recipients. With the exception of Received, the values of multiple fields are merged, so two To fields produce one list of primary recipients.

The body is normally one IA5 text body part with the repertoire set to the default. If no specific 1988 features are used the IPM is encoded as content type 2, and otherwise as content type 22. The chapter also gives three options for the case where a mapping would exceed an X.400 upper bound: generate the message in the natural manner and let truncation happen at the recipient, reject the inbound message, or truncate the fields to the X.400 upper bounds. Chapter 5 also covers the return of contents and the mapping in the other direction, from X.400 to RFC 822.
sections.plainLanguage: Each Internet header has a home in the X.400 heading. To becomes the primary recipients, Cc the copy recipients, From the originator, Subject the subject. Headers with no X.400 equivalent are carried in an extension field, and the body travels as one block of text.

sections.title: What the Specification Leaves Out
sections.content:
The RFC is explicit about its limits. It does not specify extensions of RFC 822 that give access to all X.400 services, it does not specify an X.400 user interface, and it does not map X.400 onto extended versions of RFC 822 with support for multimedia content. To map the X.400 services, the specification defines a number of extensions to RFC 822, which as a side effect give the 822 user access to some X.400 services, but the aim on the RFC 822 side is to preserve current service, so access to all X.400 services is deliberately not given. The memo says it would be a poor choice for X.400 implementors to use the earlier RFC 987 as an interface, because too many aspects of X.400 cannot be reached through it, and points to a specification targeted at X.400 without the RFC 822 restrictions for anyone who wants a text interface. Some optional and limited extensions in this area have proved useful and are defined in Appendix H.

The mapping defined in the document is to the full 1988 version of X.400 and not to a 1984 compatible subset, because new features of X.400 1988 give a much cleaner mapping, and Appendix G covers interworking with 1984 systems. Implementations and specifications that subset this specification are strongly discouraged.

The document ends with a single sentence on security: security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says what it does not cover: it does not give Internet mail access to every X.400 service, it does not define an X.400 user interface, and it does not carry multimedia. It also says nothing at all about security.
